target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection provides unmatched hands-on learning and is educationally valuable in ways substitutes cannot match.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same anatomical and biological concepts equally well or better, so real animal dissection is not uniquely educational.

target: AG1’s assumption that most dissection animals are already dead or are harmless byproducts.
objection: Classroom dissection is, in AG2’s view, primarily supplied by animals caught in the wild—approximately 99%—and wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity, making the supply chain inhumane and environmentally damaging.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is necessary for biology or medical training.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by major biology standards such as AP Biology or the Next Generation Science Standards, and no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals for physician training, so it is not necessary for curriculum or professional preparation.

target: AG2’s claim that simulations and synthetic models can teach anatomy and biology just as well as real dissection.
objection: Real dissection offers distinct, irreplaceable learning conditions: students directly handle real tissues, observe actual anatomical structures, build fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination, and engage in deeper structure-to-function reasoning that substitutes cannot fully replicate.

target: AG1’s reliance on the idea that animals used in dissection are already dead, which AG1 treats as making the practice morally neutral.
objection: Even if animals arrive dead, a classroom demand for dissectable carcasses still creates incentives for suppliers to obtain more animals, sustaining inhumane killing and environmental harm; therefore the practice is not morally neutral.

target: AG2’s assumption that student dissection creates meaningful additional killing pressure through the supply chain.
objection: In the dominant classroom supply chain, the animals are overwhelmingly already dead, and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts that would otherwise be discarded; if dissection mostly uses existing carcasses or byproducts, it does not meaningfully increase killing pressure.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is needed to meet core biology learning goals.
objection: Dissection is not required by the relevant curriculum standards, and alternatives can achieve the same learning outcomes without exposing students to animal harm; therefore it is not necessary for biology education.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can teach the same concepts equally well or better.
objection: Virtual and synthetic tools cannot fully replicate the tactile, manual engagement and structural variability of real tissue, so they do not provide the same hands-on skill-building or critical-thinking benefits as real dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely supports hands-on anatomy learning and is educationally unmatched.
objection: Interactive virtual and synthetic models can let students repeatedly explore anatomy with labels, feedback, zoom, and layer toggles, and may do so as well or better than single-use real specimens, so dissection is not uniquely superior.

target: AG2’s claim that virtual and synthetic tools can meet the same learning goals just as well or better.
objection: Real dissection requires students to open specimens, control cuts, and manipulate tissues in three dimensions, which develops fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and real-time problem-solving that digital substitutes cannot replicate.

target: AG1’s claim that real dissection is uniquely effective and unmatched educationally.
objection: Virtual and synthetic models let students repeatedly explore anatomy without destroying the specimen, while real dissection is limited by irreversible cutting and a single specimen, so dissection is not uniquely superior in learning value.

target: AG1’s broader justification that dissection is a good match for scientific thinking and educational goals.
objection: Dissection mainly trains procedural specimen-handling rather than inquiry-based scientific reasoning, so it is a weak fit for goals like asking questions, making predictions, and interpreting data.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is mostly just specimen-handling and not good scientific-thinking practice.
objection: Students can use dissection to identify structures, relate them to function, and practice careful observation and inquiry; it is not limited to procedural handling and can support critical thinking and structure-function reasoning.

target: AG1’s claim that most dissected animals are already dead or are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: That framing is inaccurate in AG2’s view because dissection animals are typically sourced through wild-catching, not mainly from leftover byproducts; the practice therefore depends on killing or capturing animals for classroom demand and harms biodiversity.

target: AG2’s harm-based objection that dissection is environmentally and morally problematic.
objection: Over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased, and commonly used fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so classroom dissection is usually a productive use of animals that were not newly killed for students.

target: AG1’s claim that most animals are already dead or are byproducts rather than newly obtained specimens.
objection: Approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, so the practice is tied to inhumane wild-capture that reduces local populations and biodiversity; it is not mainly a neutral byproduct stream.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection imposes avoidable harm despite the use of already-dead animals.
objection: In typical school use, over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so the avoidable-harm premise is overstated.

target: AG1’s harm-minimization assumption that animals are usually already dead or byproducts.
objection: If roughly 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught, then dissection does involve harmful sourcing that affects local populations and biodiversity, so it is not accurate to treat the death as merely pre-existing or unavoidable.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is harmful and unjustified because it uses newly killed animals.
objection: Over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased, and commonly used fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so the practice generally relies on animals that were not newly killed for the classroom.

target: AG1’s claim that most dissection animals were already dead and the practice is therefore justified.
objection: In AG2’s view, dissection typically depends on wild-caught animals rather than already-dead specimens; the continued demand incentivizes removal from local populations, so the practice does not rest on AG1’s factual assumption.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is mainly procedural and not aligned with scientific thinking.
objection: Teachers can structure dissections as inquiry by having students pose questions, make predictions, and test them through direct observation of real structures, so dissection can support scientific reasoning rather than merely specimen-handling.
